claims.text: Chemical complexity in high-entropy alloys produces intrinsic localized lattice distortions.
Localized lattice distortions act as obstacles to dislocation motion under dynamic loading.
The lattice distortions serve as intermittent dislocation-pinning sites.
Intermittent pinning promotes episodes of controlled dislocation release during dynamic loading.
The proposed pinning-and-release process enhances strain hardening while retaining plastic flow.
Relative to a less chemically complex conventional alloy, the high-entropy alloy will have higher yield strength under the specified dynamic loading conditions.
Relative to the conventional alloy, the high-entropy alloy will have a higher dynamic strain-hardening rate.
Higher strength and strain hardening will delay the onset of plastic instability in the high-entropy alloy.
The high-entropy alloy will retain improved ductility over a wider strain range than the conventional baseline alloy.
The proposed mechanism should operate in single-phase high-entropy alloys at moderate temperatures and strain rates.
Phase transformations or precipitation may prevent the proposed lattice-distortion mechanism from governing the response.
At extreme strain rates or temperatures, mechanisms other than lattice-distortion-mediated dislocation pinning may dominate.
The magnitude of strength and ductility improvements will vary with alloy composition and testing conditions.
